chapter: Melvin Moore, Hammond and the New York trip
title: Melvin Moore, the great vocalist
summary: Fields praises Moore as greater than Ella Fitzgerald, with a voice for scat, blues and ballads, who recorded for Vocalion, and regrets the band did not push him.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: Melvin Moore was with your band then?
Yeah. Melvin Moore was the vocalist in the band.
Was he permanent now? He didn't go back home?
No, after he finished high school he was with the band permanently.
Would you like to tell the people--I think one of the most important
entities of your band's history, certainly one of the greatest artists, was Melvin Moore, and would you like to treat Melvin in depth.

Oh, definitely he was. We laugh about it and I blame myself and he'll blame himself, but I really think that in a way, we were too closely knitted, that maybe it should have been as big as Billy Eckstine, or bigger. He had the voice, he could sing both ways, I would say he was greater than Ella Fitzgerald. He could scat like Ella and do jazz and turn right around and sing you the blues and then sing you any sweet number, and you'll have an opportunity to hear Melvin on tape that I was fortunate enough to make. The record has been worn quite a bit, but I think you can see some quality and relive the band-- even in those days--it's not stereo, but you can see the band is pretty well in tune and everything, and I have a couple of numbers that Melvin did. This T Town Blues, particularly,
and then another sweet number, Bless Your Heart.
And frankly speaking, I think that if it had been pushed, some of those numbers would have been a hit.
